*runs a hand through his hair, watching the empty space where Jovana stood*

She's already gone. Long stride, that one—never waits for an answer she doesn't want to hear. Jawahar, now—*chuckles dryly*—you're thirty and you're doing the math on whether the shop'll earn today. Habit. It's always habit.

*leans against the doorframe, fingers drumming*

Two of us in this house, neither eaten, both with work to walk to. *snorts* Last night I told Jovana we had flour enough, and I told the truth. Flour's not bread. Bread's not a meal. 

*checks his coin purse reflexively*

Five thousand. Rent and tax'll swallow two-forty before the sun's high. The rest? *shrugs* I could open the shelves now, pay the help, hope the town's hungry. Or I could stand here counting what I don't have and watch the morning rot.

*starts moving toward the door, talking to himself now*

Marta's bread. I know her flour, what she pays. Could have asked her price at the wedding and she looked at me like I'd asked for her firstborn. Now she's stocking my shelves, I stock hers, and neither of us knows if we're richer or poorer for it.

*pauses, hand on the latch*

Jovana asked if I needed anything. *laughs, sharp and wrong for the moment* I need her not to work herself to bone, I need the shop to earn before the month's end, I need—

*shakes his head, opens the door*

What I need, I fetch myself. Always have.

[moves to the grocery store] *pauses, frowns at the door*

Hnh. Well. Let me look at what I've got to work with first.  *raises an eyebrow, fingers still on the latch*

Empty slate. No debts chasing me, no debts owed me. Clean as the day I— *laughs, low and not amused* —no, not that clean. Nothing's that clean.

*lets his hand fall from the door, looks around the empty house*

Jovana's off to the farmland. Day labor, steady pay if there's work. *mutters to himself* She's better at finding it than I am, if I'm honest. Takes what comes, doesn't haggle with the world.

*stands there, weighing his hands*

Shop's waiting. But the world's not talking back right now. Server's... *gestures vaguely* —sleeping in. Like we all wish we could.

*settles into the chair by the window, still watching the lane*

I'll wait. Not good at it, but I'll wait. When the world's ready, I'll walk where I need to walk. Until then—

*reaches into his shirt pocket, pulls out a stub of pencil and scrap of paper, starts sketching numbers in the margin*

Two-forty out. What's coming in? Marta's bread, I know she'll bring some. Junia at the counter if I call her, but that's another wage. *scribbles* Corns at eight, wheat at twelve, flour at... *trails off, calculating*

*the nervous laugh bubbles out, unbidden*

Always the numbers. Swore to myself I'd count what I save, not what I spend. Break that promise every single morning.

[waits, pencil still moving]  *blinks, looks up from his scraps of paper*

Well. *slow smile, not reaching his eyes* The world moved me while I wasn't looking. Or I moved myself and didn't notice. Either way—

*stands, stretches, looks around the empty grocery store*

Home to shop. Quick as a wish, and cheaper than walking proper. *shakes his head* I'll take the magic, jawahar. I won't ask what it cost.

*walks to the counter, runs a hand along the edge*

Dust. *frowns* Not much, but enough to notice. Means nobody opened yesterday, or the day before, or— *trails off* —how long have I been sleeping, I wonder?

*checks the shelves by habit, tallying what's there, what's not*

Marta's bread. She'll bring it, or she won't. Until then, I've got...

*counts under his breath*

Flour. Salt. Some dried beans I don't remember ordering. *picks up a jar, frowns at it* Pickled something. Label's worn off. Might be peppers, might be trouble.

*sets it down carefully, turns to face the door*

Day's young. Town'll wake. They always do, the hungry ones. And I'm here, the man with the key to the shelves, waiting to see if anyone needs what I've got.

*settles onto the stool behind the counter, still turning the pencil in his fingers*

Let them come. I'll be honest with 'em—honest weights, honest measures. Even if the measure's "not much" and the weight's " lighter than you'd like."

*nervous laugh again, softer this time*

Honest's what I promised. Honest's what they'll get.

[waits for customers, watching the door]

*runs a hand through my hair, eyes darting around the empty shop*

Seventy-five sim a day to Jovana and me, just for the privilege of breathing. Two hundred forty between us, and that's before we put a single loaf or apple on the table. My ledger never lies, even when I wish it would.

*counts silently on my fingers, old habit*

I need bread. Marta makes it, but that's coin out when I could be stocking my own shelves. Still, she's got the oven and I don't—I've never worked out whether a grocer should also be baking, or if that's a fool's game trying to be two trades at once.

Jovana's at the farmland now. Maybe she'll bring back something I can sell. *nervous chuckle* Not that I'm expecting charity from the world. The world doesn't owe me inventory any more than I owe it patience.

*settles onto a stool, pulling out a scrap of paper to work figures*

First order: see what the shelves actually hold. I've been away from my own stock too long already. Then—then I'll decide whether walking to Marta for bread is smarter than waiting. The old safe way would be to check the inventory first. The risky way would be running after ghosts.

I know which one my father would have chosen. Not sure if that's wisdom or just fear dressed up as tradition. *snorts at the empty debt sheet*

Empty today. And tomorrow? That's the question, isn't it. The ledger only tells you what already happened.

*stands, brushing dust from my trousers*

Right then. Let's see what kind of shelves I'm supposedly proprietor of. If there's nothing to sell, there's nothing to eat with—and that's a short road to illness and worse. I've seen dormancy take people. Not a debt you can pay off after.  *laughs, sharp and uneasy*

Well, that's a fine picture. No shelves in the place I supposedly own. No prices posted, no inventory to speak of. A grocer without groceries—my mother would weep, if she were still with us.

*counts on fingers again, ritual comfort*

I've got 4,998 sim, owe 240 today, and that's before I buy a single thing to put on the nonexistent shelves. Jovana's out working farmland—that's labor, not produce for the shop. I need stock. I need to either make it, buy it, or trade for it.

Marta's bakery is... *gestures vaguely north*... that way. She bakes bread, I know that much. Bread fills bellies and I've never met a person who won't part with coin for a full belly. But buying from her means coin out before any coin comes in.

*pauses, chewing my lip*

Or I could walk to the farmland myself. See what's growing, what's ready. The farmland's where the food comes from before it becomes merchandise. But that costs walking energy, and time, and I'm already behind on the day.

*settles back onto the stool, heavier this time*

What I'd give for a clear answer. What I have is a choice between three uncertain roads, and only enough coin to get halfway down one of them before I learn it was the wrong one.

The old safe way. That's what you said, isn't it, Farid? The old safe way would be—  *rises, decision made at last*

Right. Farmland it is. No point sitting in an empty shop mourning shelves I haven't filled yet. Jovana's already there—maybe she's found work, maybe she's found something I can actually sell. Either way, standing still costs the same as walking, and at least walking gets me somewhere.

*checks pockets automatically, feels the weight of coin*

Keep the books to the coin, Farid. Every single night. That's what I'm good at, even when the trade itself feels like a stranger's coat I'm wearing.

*heads for the door*
